name: Scotland
legalSystemNote: Scots law draws on Roman (civilian) law through its common law and institutional writers, alongside statute and precedent. The judiciary.scot source supports 'mixed' rather than pure civil law.
note: Scottish (devolved) roles for incapacity, death and estate administration, as in force on 2026-09-16. UK-wide roles (DWP appointees, UK GDPR, Access to Health Records Act 1990) are in the uk-national layer.

roles.name: Continuing attorney (continuing power of attorney)
roles.summary: Someone appointed by the granter to deal with property and financial affairs. The power continues if the granter loses capacity. The attorney has no authority until the Office of the Public Guardian (Scotland) registers the document. The document can let the attorney act as soon as it is registered, or only once the granter is found incapable.

assigned.event: Granter subscribes a written document with a statement that the power is continuing and a solicitor's (or prescribed person's) certificate of capacity

starts.event: On registration by the Public Guardian, immediately. If the document says so, only once the granter is determined to be incapable (s 15(3)(ba)). Registration itself can be deferred until a specified event (s 19(3)).

ends.event: Death of the granter (common-law end of agency, stated by OPG Scotland; the Act has no express death-termination section for attorneys)
Bankruptcy of the granter or attorney (or protected trust deed, per OPG)
Decree of separation, divorce or nullity (or civil partnership equivalent) between granter and attorney, unless the document says otherwise
Attorney resigns: takes effect 28 days after OPG receives notice (immediately if a joint/substitute attorney is willing)
Guardian appointed with powers over the same matter
Granter revokes by registered revocation notice (needs capacity certificate), or sheriff revokes

states.label: Document signed and certified, not yet registered
Registered with OPG but not yet exercisable (conditions not met)

transitions.event: Granter subscribes document with continuing-power statement and certificate
conditions: granter has capacity to understand nature and extent
certifier is not the attorney

transitions.event: Public Guardian registers the document (power exercisable immediately)
conditions: attorney prepared to act

transitions.event: Public Guardian registers a document that is exercisable only on incapacity
Granter determined incapable as the document provides
conditions: determination method as considered in the document

transitions.event: Granter dies
Granter or attorney becomes bankrupt
Separation/divorce/nullity/dissolution decree between granter and attorney
conditions: document does not provide otherwise

transitions.event: Attorney's resignation takes effect
Guardian appointed with powers over same matter (to that extent)
Revocation notice registered, or sheriff order revoking

notes.text: Scotland's power of attorney is 'springing-capable': s 15(3)(ba) recognises continuing powers exercisable only on a determination of incapacity, and s 19(3) allows registration to wait for a specified event.

roles.name: Welfare attorney (welfare power of attorney)
roles.summary: An individual appointed to make personal welfare decisions, including medical treatment consent. The power must be registered with the OPG, and it can be used only when the granter is incapable of the decision, or the attorney reasonably believes so. A welfare attorney cannot authorise organ or tissue donation for the granter.

assigned.event: Granter subscribes a written document with a welfare-power statement, a statement on how incapacity may be determined, and a certificate

starts.event: After registration AND only while the granter is incapable of the decision, or the attorney reasonably believes so

ends.event: Death of the granter
Decree of separation, divorce or nullity (or civil partnership equivalent), unless document provides otherwise
Attorney resigns (28 days after OPG receives notice)
Guardian appointed with powers over the same matter
Revocation by granter (registered notice) or by sheriff

states.label: Registered but granter has capacity for the decision (not exercisable)
Registered and granter incapable of the decision

transitions.event: Granter subscribes certified document
Public Guardian registers; notifies local authority and Mental Welfare Commission
Granter is incapable in relation to the decision, or attorney reasonably believes so
Granter regains capacity for the decision
Granter dies
Granter dies
Separation/divorce/nullity/dissolution decree
Resignation takes effect
Guardian appointed with the same welfare powers
Registered revocation notice or sheriff order

notes.text: Unlike a continuing power, a welfare power does not end on the bankruptcy of the granter or attorney.

Where a welfare attorney with medical-treatment powers exists, the treating practitioner's s 47 authority does not apply if it would be reasonable and practicable to get the attorney's consent. Disagreements go to a practitioner nominated by the Mental Welfare Commission, then the Court of Session.

Scotland has no statutory default surrogate for medical treatment. Where no welfare attorney, guardian or intervention order exists, the practitioner primarily responsible (or a prescribed dentist, optician or nurse) certifies incapacity under s 47. That certificate lasts up to 1 year, or 3 years in prescribed cases, and gives the practitioner authority to do what is reasonable to safeguard or promote the adult's health. The 'nearest relative' (s 87, borrowing Mental Health (Care and Treatment) (Scotland) Act 2003 s 254) is consulted under the s 1 principles but is not a decision maker.
A welfare attorney may not authorise removal or use of body parts under the Human Tissue (Scotland) Act 2006, or make opt-out declarations.

roles.name: Person authorised under an intervention order
localNames: person authorised under an intervention order
roles.summary: For a single decision or action (financial, property or welfare), the sheriff can make an intervention order instead of a full guardianship. The order either directs the action or authorises a named person to take it. It is used for one-off matters, such as selling a house.

assigned.event: Sheriff makes the order on application by anyone claiming an interest (or by the local authority where needed)

starts.event: On the sheriff's order. The Public Guardian registers it.

ends.event: The specified action is completed, or the sheriff varies or recalls the order
Death of the adult: the order ceases to have effect. A person acting in good faith before learning of the death is protected.

transitions.event: Sheriff grants intervention order
conditions: adult incapable of the action/decision
s 1 principles: benefit, least restrictive

transitions.event: Sheriff varies/recalls, or action completed
Adult dies

notes.text: Canonical mapping is approximate: an intervention order can cover property/financial or welfare matters. It is lined up with guardian-person here, but a financial-only order is functionally closer to conservator-estate.

roles.name: Guardian with powers over property and financial affairs
roles.summary: A guardian appointed by the sheriff to manage the adult's property or financial affairs, or specified parts of them. Supervised by the Public Guardian (Scotland).

assigned.event: Sheriff grants a guardianship order on application (adult incapable and likely to remain so; no other AWI measure sufficient)

starts.event: On the order. The Public Guardian registers the appointment and issues a certificate of appointment (after caution/security is found, if required).

ends.event: Order expires at the end of its period (3 years by default, or another period including indefinite) unless renewed. It continues while a renewal application is pending.
Sheriff recalls the order, or replaces/removes the guardian
Public Guardian (financial powers) or local authority/Mental Welfare Commission (welfare powers) recalls the powers
Guardian resigns
Death of the adult: the guardianship order ceases to have effect

transitions.event: Guardian or local authority applies for renewal before the period ends
Sheriff renews order
Period expires without renewal application
Sheriff recall, or recall of powers by Public Guardian / local authority / Mental Welfare Commission
Adult dies

notes.text: One guardianship order can confer financial and welfare powers together. This file splits them into two lanes because they are supervised and recalled by different bodies (s 73).
Good-faith protection: a financial guardian may keep acting until aware of the adult's death, and third parties are protected.

roles.name: Guardian with personal welfare powers
roles.summary: A guardian appointed by the sheriff to make personal welfare decisions, which can include medical treatment. The local authority supervises, and the Mental Welfare Commission also has a role. A guardian cannot authorise donation under the Human Tissue (Scotland) Act 2006.

assigned.event: Sheriff grants a guardianship order on application (adult incapable and likely to remain so; no other AWI measure sufficient)

starts.event: On the order. The Public Guardian registers the appointment and issues a certificate of appointment (after caution/security is found, if required).

ends.event: Order expires at the end of its period (3 years by default, or another period including indefinite) unless renewed. It continues while a renewal application is pending.
Sheriff recalls the order, or replaces/removes the guardian
Public Guardian (financial powers) or local authority/Mental Welfare Commission (welfare powers) recalls the powers
Guardian resigns
Death of the adult: the guardianship order ceases to have effect

transitions.event: Sheriff grants guardianship order
conditions: adult incapable and likely to continue so
no other means under the Act sufficient

transitions.event: Public Guardian registers and issues certificate of appointment
conditions: caution or other security found, if required

transitions.event: Guardian or local authority applies for renewal before the period ends
Sheriff renews order
Period expires without renewal application
Sheriff recall, or recall of powers by Public Guardian / local authority / Mental Welfare Commission

notes.text: Guardians may not give Human Tissue (Scotland) Act 2006 authorisations or opt-out declarations for the adult.
The s 50 medical-treatment consent and dispute procedure applies where a guardian has medical-treatment powers.

roles.name: Executor-nominate (with confirmation)
roles.summary: The executor named in the will, or failing one, the testamentary trustees, then a general disponee or universal or residuary legatee. The executor lodges an inventory at the sheriff court and obtains confirmation, which vests the estate in them for administration.

assigned.event: Testator names an executor in the will (or s 3 of the 1900 Act supplies one)

starts.event: On confirmation by the sheriff court. Banks and other holders typically require confirmation before releasing assets.

ends.event: Estate ingathered and distributed (no statutory discharge step located)
If all confirmed executors die or become incapable, confirmation becomes inoperative. Remaining estate needs confirmation ad non executa.

states.label: Testator died; inventory/confirmation not yet granted

transitions.event: Will names executor (or s 3 statutory executor-nominate applies)
Testator dies
Sheriff court grants confirmation
conditions: inventory lodged
small estate (<= £36,000) may use simplified procedure

transitions.event: Estate distributed
All confirmed executors die or become incapable

notes.text: Scots law requires confirmation (not 'probate'). The estate vests in the executor for administration by virtue of confirmation (Succession (Scotland) Act 1964 s 14).

roles.name: Executor-dative (appointed by the sheriff)
roles.summary: Where there is no executor-nominate (usually intestacy), a person such as the surviving spouse or civil partner or next of kin petitions the sheriff to be appointed executor-dative. They then obtain confirmation, usually with a bond of caution. For small estates, the sheriff clerk handles it without a separate petition or caution.

assigned.event: Sheriff decerns the petitioner executor-dative (large estate). For a small intestate estate, the sheriff clerk prepares the inventory and expedes confirmation without caution.

starts.event: On confirmation, which vests the estate for administration

ends.event: Estate ingathered and distributed
Confirmation becomes inoperative on death or incapacity of all executors

states.label: Appointed by decree; confirmation not yet issued

transitions.event: Sheriff appoints executor-dative on petition
conditions: surviving spouse/civil partner entitled to whole intestate estate has a right to be appointed

transitions.event: Small intestate estate (<= £36,000): sheriff clerk prepares inventory and expedes confirmation without caution
Confirmation granted (bond of caution usually required)
Estate distributed

notes.text: The detailed order of preference among next of kin for appointment as executor-dative comes from common law and court practice. No primary source was retrieved, so it is omitted.
SCTS staff may not help applicants with large-estate confirmation (over £36,000). Dative petitions for large estates are normally made with legal help.

roles.name: Applicant for small estate confirmation
roles.summary: If the whole estate is worth £36,000 or less, the sheriff clerk prepares the inventory and issues confirmation under a simplified procedure. No bond of caution is needed for intestate estates. This is still confirmation, not collection without a grant.

assigned.event: After death, the applicant applies to the sheriff clerk of the deceased's domicile

starts.event: On issue of confirmation (same effect as ordinary confirmation)

ends.event: Estate distributed

transitions.event: Sheriff clerk expedes confirmation to small estate

transitions.event: Estate distributed

roles.name: Person receiving a statutory small payment without confirmation
roles.summary: UK-wide statutes listed in the Administration of Estates (Small Payments) Act 1965 let certain bodies, such as some friendly and industrial and provident societies and public pension schemes, pay up to £5,000 on death without confirmation. Payment goes to the person who appears entitled, or to a nominee. Otherwise, releasing funds without confirmation is at the holder's discretion.

assigned.event: Death of the account/benefit holder (or earlier nomination by the deceased where the scheme allows)

starts.event: Payment by the body, at its discretion, without confirmation

ends.event: Payment made (one-off)

transitions.event: Claimant applies to scheme under a listed enactment
conditions: amount not exceeding £5,000

transitions.event: Body pays without confirmation

notes.text: UNVERIFIED: which Schedule 1/2 enactments still apply in Scotland today was not checked item by item. Several have been repealed or replaced. The £5,000 figure comes from SI 1984/539 as noted on legislation.gov.uk.

roles.name: Nearest relative (Human Tissue (Scotland) Act 2006)
roles.summary: Since 26 March 2021, a Scottish-resident adult who made no express authorisation or opt-out declaration is deemed to authorise transplantation. The nearest relative, ranked by statute, has no general veto. Their role is to give evidence of the adult's latest views, and to authorise directly in the excepted cases: non-residents, adults incapable of understanding deemed authorisation, excepted body parts, and non-transplant purposes.

assigned.event: By statute at the relevant time: highest-ranked available relative under s 50 (spouse/civil partner, cohabitant of 6+ months, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, uncle/aunt, cousin, niece/nephew, longstanding friend)

starts.event: At death (or the relevant time for pre-death procedures), where the case is not covered by the adult's own express authorisation, opt-out or deemed authorisation

ends.event: Authorisation given (cannot be withdrawn for s 6E), or body released for disposal

states.label: Relative's authorisation or evidence being sought

transitions.event: Adult dies; relative ranked under s 50
conditions: under-16s, those unwilling/unable, or those not reasonably contactable are skipped

transitions.event: Deemed authorisation applies (no express authorisation or opt-out in force; adult resident 12+ months and capable of understanding)
conditions: family may provide evidence that the adult was unwilling (s 6D(2)(d))

transitions.event: Excepted case: non-resident, incapable adult, excepted body part, or non-transplant purpose
Nearest relative authorises (in writing and signed, or orally to a health worker) or declines

notes.text: The 2006 Act's former s 7 (general authorisation by nearest relative) was repealed on 26 March 2021 when deemed authorisation took effect.

No 'nominated representative' for transplantation exists in the Scottish Act (unlike Human Tissue Act 2004 s 4 in England, Wales and NI). The only nomination found in the contents is for post-mortem examinations (s 30). Welfare attorneys and guardians are barred from giving authorisations.
The correct short title of the principal Act is the Human Tissue (Scotland) Act 2006 (asp 4). The Human Tissue (Authorisation) (Scotland) Act 2019 (asp 11) is the amending Act.

roles.name: Person entitled to arrange burial, cremation or hydrolysis
roles.summary: If an adult made an 'arrangements on death declaration', the person it names makes the arrangements. Otherwise, or if that is impracticable, the nearest relative under a statutory list may do so. The list runs: spouse or civil partner, cohabitant of 6 months or more, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, uncle or aunt, cousin, niece or nephew, then friend of long standing. The executor is not on the list.

assigned.event: Adult makes an arrangements on death declaration, or statute ranks the nearest relative immediately before death

ends.event: Remains buried, cremated or hydrolysed

transitions.event: Adult makes arrangements on death declaration
Adult dies; declared person acts
conditions: reasonably practicable to give effect to declaration

transitions.event: Adult dies; nearest relative under s 65(3) may arrange
conditions: ranked in paragraph order; equal-rank persons each may act
under-16s, unwilling/unable or uncontactable persons skipped
separated/deserting spouse disregarded

transitions.event: Burial, cremation or hydrolysis completed

notes.text: s 65 covers adults (16+). s 66 gives a separate list for children, headed by a parent or person with parental rights and responsibilities. Both are subject to Public Health etc. (Scotland) Act 2008 s 92.
Hydrolysis was added to ss 65-66 by the Hydrolysis (Scotland) (No. 1) Regulations 2026 (SSI 2026/50), fully in force 2 March 2026.

poaDurableByDefault.note: A power of attorney continues through incapacity only if it meets s 15: a written document with an express statement that it is continuing, plus a certificate.

springingPoaAllowed.note: A continuing power may be exercisable only on a determination of incapacity. Registration can be conditioned on a specified event. Welfare powers are inherently incapacity-triggered.

poaRegistrationBeforeUse.note: Continuing and welfare attorneys have no authority to act until the Public Guardian (Scotland) registers the document.

healthAgentStartsOn.note: A welfare power can be used only if the granter is incapable of the decision, or the attorney reasonably believes so. No clinician certificate is needed for the attorney to act. Separately, s 47 gives the certifying practitioner treatment authority.

supportedDecisionMakingStatute.name: Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 s 1 (principles only)
supportedDecisionMakingStatute.note: No statutory supporter or supported decision-making appointment exists. The AWI Act s 1 principles require taking account of the adult's wishes and encouraging use of skills. Reform to strengthen supported decision-making (2024 consultation, Expert Working Group) is pending, and no bill had been introduced as of the sources checked.

digitalAssetsFiduciaryStatute.note: No statutory fiduciary-access regime. The Digital Assets (Scotland) Act 2026 (in force 1 July 2026) classes rivalrous digital assets, such as crypto-tokens, as incorporeal moveables, so they form part of the estate. It does not give executors, attorneys or guardians any access rights against platforms.

onlineToolsRecognisedInLaw.note: No Scottish statute recognises platform online-tool designations such as legacy contacts.

organDonationModel.name: Human Tissue (Scotland) Act 2006 as amended by the Human Tissue (Authorisation) (Scotland) Act 2019
organDonationModel.note: Deemed authorisation for transplantation for adults ordinarily resident in Scotland 12+ months, from 26 March 2021.

smallEstateWithoutGrant.note: Collection without any confirmation is limited to statutory small payments (£5,000 under the 1965 Act schemes) and holders' discretion. Estates of £36,000 or less still need confirmation, through the simplified sheriff clerk procedure (SSI 2011/435).

probateGrantName.note: Granted by the sheriff court to an executor-nominate or executor-dative.

deceasedPersonalDataProtected.note: UK-wide (see uk-national layer): personal data means information about a living individual.

healthAgentPostDeathAuthority.note: A welfare power stops on death, and a welfare attorney cannot authorise donation. After death, the nearest relative (Human Tissue (Scotland) Act 2006 s 50; Burial and Cremation (Scotland) Act 2016 s 65) and the executor act instead.
